title: Probability for insurance: risk pooling, segmentation and solidarity
text:
In the previous chapter, we studied insurance from the policyholder’s point of view: why would a risk-averse individual pay to transfer a loss, and which contract would they choose? We now turn to the insurer, which collects premiums and pays claims. Understanding the resulting risk requires studying the distribution of these claims. In this chapter, we focus on expectation and variance, the quantities associated with the first two moments. Although they do not determine the whole distribution, they provide a basis for pure-premium pricing, explain the effect of pooling, and help bound the probability of losses exceeding a given threshold.
We begin by revisiting familiar probability concepts from an insurance perspective, before developing conditional expectation in greater detail. This allows us to distinguish uncertainty within groups of similar risks from differences in expected costs between groups. We shall use this distinction to clarify the respective roles of mutualisation and solidarity: pooling shares the uncertainty of individual losses, while premiums that do not fully reflect differences in expected costs create transfers between lower- and higher-expected-cost policyholders.


We work on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), within the classical measure-theoretic framework of probability associated with Borel and Kolmogorov. We shall not need advanced results from measure theory. Recall that \(\Omega\) is the set of possible outcomes, \(\mathcal F\) is a sigma-algebra of events, and \(\mathbb P\) is a probability measure on \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\).1






NoteFrom games of chance to the modern framework





The correspondence between Pascal and Fermat in 1654, notably on how to divide the stakes of an interrupted game, is a landmark in the development of probability. Huygens gave expectation a central role in his 1657 treatise on games of chance. In the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, probability developed into a broader mathematical theory, brought together in Laplace’s Théorie analytique des probabilités (1812). Around the turn of the twentieth century, Borel’s work on measure and Lebesgue’s theory of integration supplied tools for treating continuous distributions and infinite collections of outcomes. Kolmogorov’s Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung (1933) then established the measure-theoretic axiomatic framework used today.2



A real-valued random variable is a measurable map from \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\) to \((\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))\). Here \(\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\) is the Borel sigma-algebra of \(\mathbb R\), the smallest sigma-algebra containing all open intervals. Its elements are called Borel sets; they include in particular intervals, singletons, open and closed sets, and their countable unions and intersections. No detailed knowledge of their construction will be needed: the subsets of \(\mathbb R\) used in this course will all be Borel sets. We shall also use \(\mathcal B(p)\) for the Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(p\); the argument makes the meaning of the notation unambiguous.



We assume that expectation and variance are already familiar. We recall only the conventions needed below. A random variable \(X\) is integrable, or belongs to \(L^1\), when \(\mathbb E[|X|]\) is finite; its expectation \(\mathbb E[X]\) is then well defined and finite.
In insurance, \(X\) typically represents a nonnegative monetary loss: for example, the cost of a particular claim or the total claims paid under a policy over a given period (for instance one year). For a nonnegative random variable, the expectation is always defined, possibly equal to \(+\infty\). Thus \(X\in L^1\) simply means \(\mathbb E[X]<+\infty\). The same conclusion holds for variables bounded below by a finite constant, since their negative part is bounded.



The cumulative distribution function, often abbreviated to cdf, of \(X\) is
\[
F_X:x\in\mathbb R\mapsto\mathbb P(X\leq x).
\]
In French, it is called the fonction de répartition. Recall that \(F_X\) is nondecreasing and right-continuous, with
\[
\lim_{x\to-\infty}F_X(x)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\lim_{x\to+\infty}F_X(x)=1.
\]
It determines the distribution of \(X\). In particular, for \(a<b\),
\[
\mathbb P(a<X\leq b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a).
\]
The left limit \(F_X(x-)=\lim_{t\uparrow x}F_X(t)\) equals \(\mathbb P(X<x)\), so a jump at \(x\) has size
\[
F_X(x)-F_X(x-)=\mathbb P(X=x).
\]
A jump therefore represents a positive probability attached to a single value, also called an atom of the distribution.
Whenever the expectation is defined, it can also be computed from the cdf:
\[
\mathbb E[X]
=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,\mathbb P(\mathrm d\omega)
=\int_{\mathbb R}x\,\mathrm dF_X(x).
\]
The first expression is a Lebesgue integral on the probability space. The second is a Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral: we integrate over the possible values of \(X\), with respect to the probability measure determined by \(F_X\). The name combines Stieltjes’ idea of integrating against the increments of an increasing function with Lebesgue’s measure-theoretic approach to integration.3 \(\mathrm dF_X(x)\) accounts for both continuous parts and atoms; it does not in general mean \(F_X'(x)\,\mathrm dx\).



Discrete losses. If \(X\) takes distinct values in a finite or countable set \(\{x_k:k\in K\}\), its distribution is
\[
\sum_{k\in K}\mathbb P(X=x_k)\,\delta_{x_k},
\]
where \(\delta_x\) is the Dirac probability measure at \(x\). Its cdf is
\[
F_X:x\in\mathbb R\mapsto
\sum_{k\in K}\mathbb P(X=x_k)\mathbf 1_{\{x_k\leq x\}},
\]
and its expectation (when it is well defined) is
\[
\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{k\in K}x_k\mathbb P(X=x_k).
\]
The Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral is therefore a sum weighted by the sizes of the jumps of \(F_X\).
Losses with a density. If the distribution of \(X\) has density \(f_X\) with respect to Lebesgue measure, then its cdf is
\[
F_X:x\in\mathbb R\mapsto\int_{-\infty}^x f_X(t)\,\mathrm dt,
\]
and its expectation is
\[
\mathbb E[X]=\int_{\mathbb R}x f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx.
\]
In this case \(F_X\) is absolutely continuous, \(F_X'=f_X\) Lebesgue-almost everywhere, and \(\mathrm dF_X(x)=f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\). For a nonnegative loss, the expectation integral can be restricted to \([0,\infty)\). Continuity of \(F_X\) alone does not imply the existence of a density, as the example of the devil’s staircase in the aside below illustrates.
No claim, or a claim with a continuous severity. A particularly common insurance model has distribution
\[
(1-p)\delta_0(\mathrm dx)
+p f(x)\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}}\,\mathrm dx,
\]
where \(p\in(0,1)\) is the probability of a claim and \(f\) is the density of its amount conditional on a claim occurring. In particular,
\[
f(x)\geq0\quad\text{for }x>0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\int_0^\infty f(x)\,\mathrm dx=1.
\]
The cdf is
\[
F_X:x\in\mathbb R\mapsto
\begin{cases}
0,&x<0,\\
1-p+p\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,\mathrm dt,&x\geq0,
\end{cases}
\]
and the expectation is
\[
\mathbb E[X]=p\int_0^\infty x f(x)\,\mathrm dx.
\]
Equivalently, this law can be obtained by taking \(X=BS\), where \(B\) is Bernoulli with parameter \(p\), \(S\) has density \(f\) on \((0,\infty)\), and \(B\) and \(S\) are independent.






NoteA measure-theoretic aside: densities and the devil’s staircase





A density is always relative to a reference measure. The Radon-Nikodym theorem states that if a finite measure \(\nu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to a sigma-finite measure \(\mu\), then there exists a nonnegative measurable function \(h\), unique up to equality \(\mu\)-almost everywhere, such that
\[
\nu(A)=\int_A h\,\mathrm d\mu.
\]
We write \(h=\mathrm d\nu/\mathrm d\mu\). The usual probability density uses Lebesgue measure as its reference measure. Discrete probabilities can instead be viewed as densities with respect to counting measure on a countable support.
Remark. The mixed insurance distribution above also has a density, provided we use \(\delta_0+\lambda_{(0,\infty)}\) as the reference measure, where \(\lambda_{(0,\infty)}\) is Lebesgue measure restricted to \((0,\infty)\). That density equals \(1-p\) at zero and \(pf(x)\) for \(x>0\).
More generally, the Lebesgue decomposition splits any probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R\) uniquely into
\[
\mu=\mu_{\mathrm{ac}}+\mu_{\mathrm{s}},
\]
where \(\mu_{\mathrm{ac}}\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure and \(\mu_{\mathrm{s}}\) is singular with respect to it, meaning that it is concentrated on a set of Lebesgue measure zero. The singular part can itself be decomposed uniquely into an atomic part and a singular continuous part:
\[
\mu_{\mathrm{s}}=\mu_{\mathrm{at}}+\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}.
\]
Combining the two decompositions gives
\[
\mu=\mu_{\mathrm{ac}}+\mu_{\mathrm{at}}+\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}.
\]
The atomic part \(\mu_{\mathrm{at}}\) is the finite or countable sum of the masses at individual points. The singular continuous part \(\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}\) has no atoms, but is still concentrated on a set of Lebesgue measure zero. These three components are nonnegative measures whose total masses add up to one; they are not individually probability measures unless they carry all the mass.
The standard example of a singular continuous probability measure is the Cantor distribution. Its cumulative distribution function, the devil’s staircase, is continuous and increases from zero to one on \([0,1]\), although its derivative is zero Lebesgue-almost everywhere. The distribution is concentrated on the Cantor set, which has Lebesgue measure zero, and has no atoms.
The Cantor set consists of the numbers in \([0,1]\) that admit a base-three expansion using only the digits \(0\) and \(2\). The qualification “admit” matters at points with two expansions: for example, \(1/3=0.1_3=0.0222\ldots_3\) belongs to the set. To obtain the Cantor distribution, choose these ternary digits independently, each being \(0\) or \(2\) with probability \(1/2\). Equivalently, if \((B_n)_{n\geq1}\) are independent Bernoulli random variables with parameter \(1/2\), then
\[
C=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{2B_n}{3^n}
\]
has the Cantor distribution. Each interval retained after \(n\) steps of the middle-third construction has probability \(2^{-n}\), while their total length is \((2/3)^n\), which tends to zero.
Thus discrete distributions and distributions with a density do not exhaust all possibilities, even after taking mixtures. This is a useful warning against identifying \(\mathrm dF_X(x)\) with \(F_X'(x)\,\mathrm dx\) without absolute continuity. For the insurance models in this course, however, the singular continuous component is mainly a mathematical curiosity: discrete, absolutely continuous and mixed distributions will cover our practical needs.






The survival function of \(X\) is
\[
\overline F_X:x\in\mathbb R\mapsto\mathbb P(X>x)=1-F_X(x).
\]

Proposition 1 (Expectation and the survival function) For every nonnegative random variable \(X\),
\[
\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(X>t)\,\mathrm dt.
\]
Both sides may be infinite. This formula applies to discrete, continuous and mixed distributions without any change.


Proof. Recall first that, for every event \(A\), the indicator \(\mathbf 1_A\) has a Bernoulli distribution:
\[
\mathbf 1_A\sim\mathcal B(\mathbb P(A))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).
\]
For every \(\omega\in\Omega\),
\[
X(\omega)=\int_0^{X(\omega)}1\,\mathrm dt
=\int_0^\infty\mathbf 1_{\{X(\omega)>t\}}\,\mathrm dt.
\]
By Fubini’s theorem in its nonnegative form, we may interchange expectation and integration. Since the integrand is nonnegative, there is no integrability condition to check, and the equality remains valid when the integrals are infinite:
\[
\mathbb E[X]
=\int_0^\infty\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{X>t\}}]\,\mathrm dt
=\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(X>t)\,\mathrm dt.
\]

For a nonnegative integer-valued loss, the formula becomes
\[
\mathbb E[X]
=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\mathbb P(X>k)
=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\mathbb P(X\geq k).
\]




Definition 1 (Pure premium) For full coverage of an integrable loss \(X\), the pure premium is
\[
\pi=\mathbb E[X].
\]
It is the expected claim cost. It does not include administrative expenses, a safety loading, remuneration of capital or profit. If a contract pays an indemnity \(I(X)\), its pure premium is \(\mathbb E[I(X)]\).

The pure premium uses only the first moment of the loss distribution. Two losses can have the same expectation and very different probabilities of producing a large claim. The second moment gives additional information about this variability; this is why we now turn to variance.

section: Variance and the probability of large losses
text:
Variance and the probability of large losses

The best constant prediction
Recall that \(X\in L^2\) means \(\mathbb E[X^2]<+\infty\) and implies \(X\in L^1\). For such a variable, write
\[
m=\mathbb E[X]\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sigma^2=\mathbb V(X)=\mathbb E[(X-m)^2] = \mathbb E[X^2] - \mathbb E[X]^2.
\]

Proposition 2 (Expectation as the best constant prediction) For \(X\in L^2\), the unique minimiser of \(c\in\mathbb R\mapsto\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\) is \(\mathbb E[X]\), and the minimum is \(\mathbb V(X)\):
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{c\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
=\mathbb E[X]\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\min_{c\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]=\mathbb V(X).
\]


Proof. For every \(c\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
&=\mathbb E[(X-m+m-c)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(X-m)^2]+2(m-c)\mathbb E[X-m]+(m-c)^2\\
&=\mathbb V(X)+(m-c)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The conclusion follows because \((m-c)^2\) is nonnegative and vanishes only at \(c=m\).

The expectation is the best constant prediction under squared error; the variance is the remaining mean squared error. This interpretation will be the starting point for conditional expectation later in the course.


Bienaymé-Chebyshev’s inequality

Theorem 1 (Bienaymé-Chebyshev’s inequality) Let \(X\in L^2\), \(m=\mathbb E[X]\) and \(\sigma^2=\mathbb V(X)\). For every \(t>0\),
\[
\mathbb P(|X-m|\geq t)\leq\frac{\sigma^2}{t^2}.
\]
If \(\sigma>0\), the equivalent formulation in units of standard deviation is
\[
\mathbb P(|X-m|\geq k\sigma)\leq\frac{1}{k^2},
\qquad k>0.
\]


Proof. Apply Markov’s inequality to the nonnegative random variable \((X-m)^2\):
\[
\mathbb P(|X-m|\geq t)
=\mathbb P((X-m)^2\geq t^2)
\leq\frac{\mathbb E[(X-m)^2]}{t^2}.
\]

A bound above one can of course be replaced by the trivial bound one.


Cantelli’s inequality: controlling an exceedance
For an insurer, a large loss above its expectation is usually more concerning than a loss equally far below it. This motivates a one-sided version of the preceding inequality.

Theorem 2 (Cantelli’s inequality) Let \(X\in L^2\), \(m=\mathbb E[X]\) and \(\sigma^2=\mathbb V(X)\). For every \(t>0\),
\[
\mathbb P(X-m\geq t)
\leq\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+t^2},\qquad t>0.
\]
If \(\sigma>0\), this can also be written as
\[
\mathbb P(X\geq m+k\sigma)\leq\frac{1}{1+k^2},\qquad k>0.
\]

For example, the probability of exceeding the mean by at least three standard deviations is at most \(1/10\), whatever the distribution with finite second moment.

Proof. Put \(Y=X-m\). For any \(a\geq0\),
\[
\{Y\geq t\}\subseteq\{(Y+a)^2\geq(t+a)^2\}.
\]
Markov’s inequality therefore yields
\[
\mathbb P(Y\geq t)
\leq\frac{\mathbb E[(Y+a)^2]}{(t+a)^2}
= \frac{\mathbb E[Y^2] + 2a\mathbb E[Y]+a^2]}{(t+a)^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2+a^2}{(t+a)^2}.
\]
If \(\sigma^2>0\), differentiation gives
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm da}
\frac{\sigma^2+a^2}{(t+a)^2}
=\frac{2(at-\sigma^2)}{(t+a)^3}.
\]
The derivative has the sign of \(at-\sigma^2\), giving the following variation table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
a
& 0 & & \dfrac{\sigma^2}{t} & & +\infty \\[6pt]
\hline
\dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm da}
\dfrac{\sigma^2+a^2}{(t+a)^2}
& & - & 0 & + & \\[10pt]
\hline
\dfrac{\sigma^2+a^2}{(t+a)^2}
& \dfrac{\sigma^2}{t^2}
& \searrow
& \dfrac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+t^2}
& \nearrow
& 1
\end{array}
\]
The minimum over \(a\geq0\) is therefore attained at \(a=\sigma^2/t\) and equals \(\sigma^2/(\sigma^2+t^2)\), hence the result. If \(\sigma^2=0\), then \(X=m\) almost surely, so the inequality holds directly.

These are concentration inequalities: they control deviations from a central value. Variance alone gives general but sometimes coarse bounds. Stronger assumptions lead to other inequalities, such as Hoeffding’s inequality for sums of independent bounded variables, or Chernoff bounds when exponential moments are available. Additional assumptions should not be taken for granted for insurance losses.

title: Probability for insurance: risk pooling, segmentation and solidarity
section: The law of large numbers and risk pooling
text:
The law of large numbers and risk pooling

A reminder on convergence






NoteAlmost sure convergence, convergence in probability and convergence in \(L^1\)



Let \((X_n)_{n\geq1}\) be a sequence of random variables and let \(X\) be a random variable on the same probability space.

Almost sure convergence, written \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}X\), means that
\[
\mathbb P\!\left(\left\{\omega\in\Omega:\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(\omega)=X(\omega)\right\}\right)=1.
\]
Convergence in probability, written \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}X\), means that
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0,\qquad\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Convergence in \(L^1\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{L^1}X\), means that \(X_n,X\in L^1\) and
\[
\mathbb E[|X_n-X|]\longrightarrow0.
\]

The following triangle records the main implications. On the upward arrow on the left, almost sure convergence holds along a subsequence, not necessarily along the whole sequence.

A sequence \((X_n)_{n\geq1}\) of integrable random variables is uniformly integrable if
\[
\lim_{K\to\infty}\sup_{n\geq1}
\mathbb E\!\left[|X_n|\mathbf 1_{\{|X_n|>K\}}\right]=0.
\]
If \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}X\) and \((X_n)_{n\geq1}\) is uniformly integrable, then \(X\in L^1\) and \(X_n\xrightarrow{L^1}X\). Conversely, convergence in \(L^1\) implies uniform integrability. Almost sure convergence alone does not imply convergence in \(L^1\), and convergence in \(L^1\) alone does not imply almost sure convergence of the whole sequence.
The dominated convergence theorem is an important special case: if \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}X\) and \(|X_n|\leq U\) almost surely for every \(n\), where \(U\in L^1\), then the sequence is uniformly integrable and \(X_n\xrightarrow{L^1}X\).
The subsequence statement can be strengthened: \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}X\) if and only if every subsequence has a further subsequence converging almost surely to \(X\). For exercises and proofs, see the problems on almost sure convergence and convergence in probability and uniform integrability on I Love Proba.




The law of large numbers in \(L^1\)

Theorem 3 (Law of large numbers) Let \((X_i)_{i\geq1}\) be independent and identically distributed random variables with \(X_1\in L^1\). Then
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i
\xrightarrow{\mathbb P,\,\mathrm{a.s.},\,L^1}\mathbb E[X_1].
\]

A finite variance is not required. For a guided proof, see the problem From weak to strong: around the law of large numbers on I Love Proba.


Why a large portfolio helps
Let \(X_i\) be the annual claim cost of policyholder \(i\). If these costs are i.i.d. and integrable, the average claim cost converges to \(\mathbb E[X_1]\). Charging this pure premium for every policy gives the insurer the following net claim cost per policy:
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i-\mathbb E[X_1]\bigr)
\xrightarrow{\mathbb P,\,\mathrm{a.s.},\,L^1}0.
\]
This is the basic principle of risk pooling, also called mutualisation: individual uncertainty becomes more predictable when we consider an average over many risks.
The effect is particularly transparent for square-integrable losses. If \(X_1\in L^2\) and \(\sigma^2=\mathbb V(X_1)\), then
\[
\mathbb V\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb V\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right)=n\sigma^2.
\]
The variance of the average decreases, even though the variance of the total increases. For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the Bienaymé-Chebyshev inequality gives
\[
\mathbb P\!\left(\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i-\mathbb E[X_1]\right|\geq\varepsilon\right)
\leq\frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}.
\]
If we are interested specifically in claims exceeding the premiums collected by at least \(\varepsilon\) per policy, Cantelli’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb P\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\geq\mathbb E[X_1]+\varepsilon\right)
\leq\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n\varepsilon^2}.
\]


What does independence mean in insurance?
Independence may be a reasonable approximation for some geographically dispersed accidental mobile-phone damage claims or isolated water leaks in unrelated buildings. Even there it is an assumption to examine: a common product defect, shared infrastructure or a weather event can create dependence.
For floods, earthquakes or storms, many claims may arise from the same event. A larger portfolio concentrated in the affected area may therefore produce more claims from the same catastrophe, rather than more opportunities for independent losses to offset one another. More generally,
\[
\mathbb V\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right)
=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb V(X_i)
+\frac2{n^2}\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).
\]
The covariance terms can prevent concentration. For example, if all variances equal \(\sigma^2>0\) and every distinct pair has the same correlation \(\rho\geq0\), then
\[
\mathbb V\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right)
=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\rho\frac{n-1}{n}\right)
\longrightarrow\rho\sigma^2.
\]
A common source of uncertainty cannot be eliminated merely by adding more policies exposed to it.

Exercise 1 (Pooling in the presence of a common source of risk) Let \(U,V_1,V_2,\ldots\) be independent, nonnegative, square-integrable random variables, with \((V_i)_{i\geq1}\) identically distributed. Suppose
\[
\mathbb V(U)=\rho\sigma^2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb V(V_i)=(1-\rho)\sigma^2,
\]
where \(\sigma>0\) and \(\rho\in[0,1]\). Define \(X_i=U+V_i\): \(U\) is a common loss component, while \(V_i\) is specific to policyholder \(i\).

Show that \(\mathbb V(X_i)=\sigma^2\) and that \(\operatorname{Corr}(X_i,X_j)=\rho\) for \(i\ne j\).
Compute the variance of \(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Deduce from the Bienaymé-Chebyshev inequality that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\mathbb P\!\left(\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i-\mathbb E[X_1]\right|\geq\varepsilon\right)
\leq\frac{\sigma^2}{\varepsilon^2}\left(\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{n}\right).
\]
Use the law of large numbers for \((V_i)_{i\geq1}\) to identify the almost sure limit of \(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Explain why the common source of uncertainty remains when \(\rho>0\).




Identically distributed risks: heterogeneity and segmentation
The assumption of identical distributions raises a more subtle question. Some differences are so obvious that we would not naturally put the risks in the same category: a factory and a small shop have different exposures, as do a modest flat and a large industrial building. Even within motor insurance, vehicle value, mileage and driving experience provide immediate reasons to distinguish expected claim costs.
Other differences remain within a product sold on common terms. Consider two travellers visiting the same destination for the same duration: one plans to visit museums, the other to take part in more hazardous outdoor activities. They may nevertheless buy the same package, perhaps included with a booking or a bank card, without being offered a contract tailored to their activities. Likewise, people living in similar homes can differ in their precautions against water damage. A common contract does not imply a common loss distribution.
We should distinguish two questions. Prediction asks which characteristics help explain claims. Pricing asks which of those characteristics the insurer can and chooses to use when setting premiums. A characteristic may be informative but unavailable, too costly to measure, or deliberately excluded because using it would be considered undesirable.
Segmentation uses information about risks to distinguish groups of policyholders. It can affect premiums, deductibles, coverage limits or eligibility for cover. For example, an insurer might cover ordinary holiday activities under a standard travel policy but require a separate agreement for high-altitude mountaineering. Insurers may also encourage prevention through financial incentives: some US health plans reimburse qualifying fitness expenses subject to evidence of regular participation. This is an incentive attached to the plan, rather than necessarily a reduction in the insurance premium.4
Information available at inception supports a priori pricing; claims observed during the contract can support a posteriori adjustments. The French bonus-malus system in motor insurance is a familiar example: a coefficient applied to the reference premium evolves with the policyholder’s history of claims involving liability. In the usual case, a year without an at-fault accident reduces the coefficient by 5%, while a fully at-fault accident increases it by 25%, subject to the system’s limits and exceptions.5 Hereafter, we focus on segmentation through premiums while keeping coverage fixed.
Informally, segmentation resembles clustering: we group together risks that appear sufficiently similar and use observations from a group to learn about its members. This does not mean that every pricing model is a clustering algorithm; characteristics may also enter a model continuously.
Finer segmentation has a cost. With a fixed amount of data, dividing a portfolio into more groups leaves fewer observations in each group. Estimates of claim frequencies and average severities then become less precise. Coarser groups provide more observations but conceal more heterogeneity. There is a trade-off between distinguishing risk profiles and estimating their costs reliably.
Heterogeneity also raises the question of solidarity. If all travellers pay the same premium despite different planned activities, those with lower expected costs partly finance those with higher expected costs. A common premium can similarly create transfers between more and less cautious policyholders. In health insurance, such transfers may be a deliberate objective: people in good health contribute towards the expected costs of people with chronic illnesses. A higher expected cost need not result from a choice or a lack of care. Solidarity can therefore be both intentional and desirable; it can also arise simply because relevant differences are not observed.
These transfers differ from sharing chance losses between otherwise comparable people. To make the distinction precise, we need conditional expectation. It also clarifies an apparent paradox: policyholders drawn independently from the same heterogeneous population can have the same unconditional loss distribution, even though their loss distributions differ once their characteristics are known.

title: Probability for insurance: risk pooling, segmentation and solidarity
text:
Conditional expectation: prediction using information

The discrete intuition
Let \(X\in L^1\) and suppose that a real-valued characteristic \(Y\) takes values in a finite or countable set. Denote the set of its atoms by
\[
A_Y=\{y\in\mathbb R:\mathbb P(Y=y)>0\}.
\]
For these values, define the conditional mean function
\[
g:y\in A_Y\mapsto\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]
=\frac{\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{Y=y\}}]}{\mathbb P(Y=y)}.
\]
If \(X\) is also discrete, this becomes
\[
g(y)=\sum_x x\,\mathbb P(X=x\mid Y=y).
\]
The number \(g(y)\) is the average loss within group \(y\). Before we know the policyholder’s group, the corresponding prediction is the random variable \(g(Y)\), denoted by
\[
\mathbb E[X\mid Y]=g(Y).
\]
We may set \(g(y)=0\) outside \(A_Y\), since \(\mathbb P(Y\in A_Y)=1\). Notice the distinction between the number \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]\), for a specified group, and the random variable \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\), whose value depends on the group.
If \(Y\) has a continuous distribution, however, \(\mathbb P(Y=y)=0\) for every \(y\). Division by this probability is impossible. We need a construction that describes the information supplied by \(Y\) without conditioning directly on a zero-probability event.


Conditional expectation as an \(L^2\) projection
Let \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) be a sub-sigma-algebra representing available information. The main example is \(\mathcal G=\sigma(Y)\), the sigma-algebra generated by a real-valued or vector-valued random variable \(Y\).
Suppose \(X\in L^2\). Informally, we seek the best prediction of \(X\) that uses only this information. Formally, the admissible predictions are the square-integrable, \(\mathcal G\)-measurable random variables, and we measure prediction error by \(\mathbb E[(X-H)^2]\).

Definition 2 (Conditional expectation in \(L^2\)) For \(X\in L^2\), the conditional expectation of \(X\) given \(\mathcal G\), denoted by \(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\), is the minimiser, unique up to almost sure equality, of the function
\[
H\in L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,\mathbb P)\mapsto\mathbb E[(X-H)^2].
\]

When \(\mathcal G=\sigma(Y)\), we use the shorter notation
\[
\mathbb E[X\mid Y]=\mathbb E[X\mid\sigma(Y)].
\]
The minimiser exists because \(L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,\mathbb P)\) is a closed linear subspace of the Hilbert space \(L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), with inner product \(\langle U,V\rangle=\mathbb E[UV]\). Conditional expectation is the orthogonal projection onto this subspace. We shall also write \(L^2(\mathcal G)\) for \(L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,\mathbb P)\).

Proposition 3 (Orthogonality and Pythagoras) For \(X\in L^2\),
\[
\forall H\in L^2(\mathcal G),\qquad
\mathbb E\!\left[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G])H\right]=0.
\]
Consequently, for every \(H\in L^2(\mathcal G)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-H)^2]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G])^2\right]\\
&\quad+\mathbb E\!\left[(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]-H)^2\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

The plane represents the subspace \(L^2(\mathcal G)\). The right-angled triangle illustrates the Pythagorean identity above; it is a geometric representation of a Hilbert-space projection.
Thus information replaces the best constant prediction \(\mathbb E[X]\) by the best prediction measurable with respect to \(\mathcal G\). In the case \(\mathcal G=\sigma(Y)\), such a prediction can be written as a measurable function of \(Y\):
\[
\mathbb E[X\mid Y]=g(Y).
\]
The function \(g\) is determined up to equality \(\mathbb P_Y\)-almost everywhere: changing it on a set of values that \(Y\) has probability zero of visiting leaves the prediction unchanged almost surely.


The characterisation that extends beyond \(L^2\)
Writing \(M=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\) and taking \(H=\mathbf 1_A\) in the orthogonality relation gives
\[
\mathbb E[M\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_A]
\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal G.
\]
This equality only involves first moments. It provides the general definition.

Definition 3 (Conditional expectation of an integrable random variable) If \(X\in L^1\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\) is a random variable \(M\), unique up to almost sure equality, such that:

\(M\) is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable;
\(M\in L^1\);
for every \(A\in\mathcal G\),
\[
\mathbb E[M\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_A].
\]


The last property says that the prediction gets the average right on every event identifiable from the available information. Equivalently,
\[
\mathbb E[MH]=\mathbb E[XH]
\]
for every bounded \(\mathcal G\)-measurable random variable \(H\). For \(L^2\) variables this extends by approximation to \(H\in L^2(\mathcal G)\), recovering the projection characterisation.

Proof. Existence. For \(X\geq0\) integrable, the finite measure
\[
\nu:A\in\mathcal G\mapsto\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_A]
\]
is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mathbb P\) restricted to \(\mathcal G\). The Radon-Nikodym theorem gives the required nonnegative density \(M\). For a general integrable \(X\), apply the construction to \(X^+\) and \(X^-\), then subtract.
Uniqueness. If \(M\) and \(N\) satisfy the definition, use \(A=\{M>N\}\in\mathcal G\). Then
\[
\mathbb E[(M-N)\mathbf 1_{\{M>N\}}]=0,
\]
so \(M\leq N\) almost surely. Interchanging \(M\) and \(N\) proves equality almost surely.

Nonnegative random variables with possibly infinite expectation. If \(X\geq0\), define
\[
\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[X\wedge n\mid\mathcal G].
\]
Since conditional expectation preserves order, with probability one,
\[
0\leq\mathbb E[X\wedge n\mid\mathcal G]
\leq\mathbb E[X\wedge(n+1)\mid\mathcal G]
\qquad\text{for every }n\geq1.
\]
On this event of probability one, the sequence is nondecreasing, so its limit exists in \([0,\infty]\). Set the limit to zero on the exceptional event if necessary. Monotone convergence shows that the resulting random variable is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable and satisfies
\[
\forall A\in\mathcal G,\qquad
\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mathbf 1_A\right]
=\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_A],
\]
where either side may be infinite and products with an indicator are taken to be zero off the event. This characterisation determines the conditional expectation up to almost sure equality. For a random variable bounded below, subtract a finite lower bound first and add it back afterwards.
In what follows, pricing uses integrable losses and variance calculations use square-integrable losses.


Basic properties

Proposition 4 (Properties of conditional expectation) All equalities and inequalities between random variables below hold almost surely. Write \(L^1(\mathcal G)\) for the integrable, \(\mathcal G\)-measurable random variables.
Linearity.
\[
\forall X,W\in L^1,\ \forall a,b\in\mathbb R,\qquad
\mathbb E[aX+bW\mid\mathcal G]
=a\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]+b\mathbb E[W\mid\mathcal G].
\]
Positivity and monotonicity.
\[
\forall X,W\in L^1,\qquad
X\leq W\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\leq\mathbb E[W\mid\mathcal G].
\]
In particular, the conditional expectation of a nonnegative random variable is nonnegative.
Known quantities remain unchanged.
\[
\forall X\in L^1(\mathcal G),\qquad\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]=X.
\]
Taking out known factors. For every bounded, \(\mathcal G\)-measurable random variable \(H\),
\[
\forall X\in L^1,\qquad\mathbb E[HX\mid\mathcal G]=H\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G].
\]
The same equality holds for \(X\in L^2\) and \(H\in L^2(\mathcal G)\), even if \(H\) is unbounded.
Preservation of expectation.
\[
\forall X\in L^1,\qquad\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]]=\mathbb E[X].
\]
Tower property. If \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\) is a sub-sigma-algebra, then
\[
\forall X\in L^1,\qquad
\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H\right]
=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal H].
\]
Independent information.
\[
\forall X\in L^1,\qquad
X\text{ independent of }\mathcal G
\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]=\mathbb E[X].
\]
Positivity, monotonicity, preservation of expectation and the tower property also hold for nonnegative random variables with possibly infinite expectations.



Recovering the discrete formula
Suppose \(Y\) takes values in a finite or countable set, and use the set \(A_Y\) and the function \(g\) defined earlier. Then
\[
\mathbb E[|g(Y)|]
\leq\sum_{y\in A_Y}\mathbb E[|X|\mathbf 1_{\{Y=y\}}]
=\mathbb E[|X|].
\]
Moreover, for every subset \(B\) of \(A_Y\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[g(Y)\mathbf 1_{\{Y\in B\}}]
&=\sum_{y\in B}g(y)\mathbb P(Y=y)\\
&=\sum_{y\in B}\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{Y=y\}}]\\
&=\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{Y\in B\}}].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(g(Y)\) satisfies the characterisation and is indeed \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\). Values assigned to \(g(y)\) when \(\mathbb P(Y=y)=0\) do not affect the resulting random variable.


The case of a joint density
Suppose \((X,Y)\), with \(Y\) taking values in \(\mathbb R^d\), has a joint Lebesgue density \(f_{X,Y}\), and \(X\in L^1\). The marginal density of \(Y\) is
\[
f_Y:y\in\mathbb R^d\mapsto\int_{\mathbb R}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm dx.
\]
Define the set on which the conditional mean formula is well defined:
\[
D_Y=\left\{y\in\mathbb R^d:
0<f_Y(y)<\infty\ \text{and}\
\int_{\mathbb R}|x|f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm dx<\infty\right\}.
\]
Fubini’s theorem and \(X\in L^1\) imply that \(\mathbb P(Y\in D_Y)=1\). For \(y\in D_Y\), the conditional density is
\[
f_{X\mid Y=y}:x\in\mathbb R\mapsto\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},
\]
and we define
\[
g:y\in D_Y\mapsto\int_{\mathbb R}x f_{X\mid Y=y}(x)\,\mathrm dx.
\]
Set \(g(y)=0\) outside \(D_Y\). Then \(\mathbb E[|g(Y)|]\leq\mathbb E[|X|]\). For every bounded measurable function \(h:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), Fubini’s theorem also gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[g(Y)h(Y)]
&=\int_{\mathbb R^d}h(y)\left(\int_{\mathbb R}x f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm dx\right)\mathrm dy\\
&=\mathbb E[Xh(Y)].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(g(Y)=\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\). We write \(g(y)=\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]\), understanding that this function is determined only \(\mathbb P_Y\)-almost everywhere. When \(\mathbb P(Y=y)=0\), this notation refers to the conditional mean function, not to division by the probability of the event \(\{Y=y\}\).
An insurance loss with an atom at zero does not satisfy the joint-density assumption above. A common conditional model instead specifies a claim probability \(p(y)\in[0,1]\) and a density \(f(\cdot\mid y)\) on \((0,\infty)\). Extend this density by zero to \((-\infty,0]\). For all real \(a\leq b\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(a\leq X\leq b\mid Y=y)
&=(1-p(y))\mathbf 1_{\{a\leq0\leq b\}}\\
&\quad+p(y)\int_a^b f(x\mid y)\,\mathrm dx.
\end{aligned}
\]
The conditional pure premium is then
\[
\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]=p(y)\int_0^\infty x f(x\mid y)\,\mathrm dx.
\]
Segmentation can therefore act through both claim frequency and claim severity.

title: Probability for insurance: risk pooling, segmentation and solidarity
text:
The law of total variance
The projection interpretation already suggests a decomposition: part of the variability of \(X\) is explained by \(Y\), and the rest remains after \(Y\) is known. We now make this precise.

Definition 4 (Conditional variance) For \(X\in L^2\), the conditional variance of \(X\) given \(Y\) is the random variable
\[
\mathbb V(X\mid Y)
=\mathbb E\!\left[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2\mid Y\right]
=\mathbb E[X^2\mid Y]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]^2.
\]

It measures residual variability within the group identified by \(Y\). Unlike the unconditional variance, it is generally a random variable: different groups can have different variances.

Theorem 4 (Law of total variance) For \(X\in L^2\),
\[
\mathbb V(X)
=\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Y)]
+\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]).
\]


Proof. Write
\[
X-\mathbb E[X]
=\bigl(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\bigr)
+\bigl(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]-\mathbb E[X]\bigr).
\]
The two terms are orthogonal. Indeed, taking out the \(Y\)-measurable factor and using preservation of expectation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E\!\left[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]-\mathbb E[X])\right]\\
&\qquad=\mathbb E\!\left[(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]-\mathbb E[X])
\mathbb E[X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\mid Y]\right]=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Squaring the decomposition and taking expectations therefore yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb V(X)
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2\right]\\
&\quad+\mathbb E\!\left[(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]-\mathbb E[X])^2\right]\\
&=\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Y)]+\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]),
\end{aligned}
\]
where we used \(\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]=\mathbb E[X]\).

The two components have distinct interpretations:

Within-group (intragroup) variance: \(\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Y)]\) is the average residual variance inside the groups.
Between-group (intergroup) variance: \(\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Y])\) measures differences in expected loss between groups.

For a finite segmentation with groups \(y_1,\ldots,y_k\), each of positive probability, the identity becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb V(X)
&=\sum_{j=1}^k\mathbb P(Y=y_j)\mathbb V(X\mid Y=y_j)\\
&\quad+\sum_{j=1}^k\mathbb P(Y=y_j)
\bigl(\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y_j]-\mathbb E[X]\bigr)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Groups can have different distributions but the same mean. In that case the between-group term is zero: this decomposition measures heterogeneity in expected costs, not every possible difference between loss distributions.

title: Probability for insurance: risk pooling, segmentation and solidarity
section: Who bears the expenditure? Pure-premium pricing
text:
Who bears the expenditure? Pure-premium pricing

The accounting convention
We now consider full insurance of a nonnegative loss \(X\in L^2\), with no expenses, loading, default or time discounting. We view \(X\) as the loss of a policyholder drawn from the population. The premium \(\pi\) is paid before the loss is realised and may depend on characteristics known at inception.
The policyholder incurs the loss \(X\), receives the indemnity \(X\), and pays \(\pi\). Their net expenditure is therefore \(\pi\). The insurer pays \(X\) and receives \(\pi\), so its net expenditure is \(X-\pi\). A negative insurer expenditure is a net receipt. Adding the two leaves the underlying loss \(X\).
For comparison, without insurance the policyholder’s expenditure would be \(X\), with expectation \(\mathbb E[X]\) and variance \(\mathbb V(X)\).


A common pure premium: no segmentation
Set \(m=\mathbb E[X]\) and charge everyone \(\pi=m\).









Party
Net expenditure
Expected net expenditure
Variance of net expenditure

The policyholder exchanges the uncertain loss for a constant payment. The insurer takes on all the variance associated with a randomly selected policy, while breaking even in expectation. Pooling many sufficiently independent policies then reduces the variability of the insurer’s average net expenditure.


Segmentation using \(Y\)
Now charge the conditional pure premium
\[
\pi=\mathbb E[X\mid Y].
\]
The premium is constant within a group but varies across groups. The table below gives unconditional moments, before the group of the randomly selected policyholder is specified.









Party
Net expenditure
Expected net expenditure
Variance of net expenditure




Policyholder
\(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\)
\(\mathbb E[X]\)
\(\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Y])\)


Insurer
\(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\)
\(0\)
\(\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Y)]\)


Total
\(X\)

\(\mathbb V(X)\)



Here the variances add because the two expenditure variables are uncorrelated:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\mathbb E[X\mid Y],X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\right)=0.
\]
Variances of payments do not add in general; the orthogonality of conditional expectation is doing the work.
Conditional on \(Y=y\), the policyholder pays the known amount \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]\), so their conditional expenditure variance is zero. The policyholder’s variance in the table is thus a measure of differences in premiums across the population, not uncertainty about the claim payment for a person whose group is already known.
Although \(X\) is nonnegative, the residual \(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\) need not have a constant lower bound when the conditional premium is unbounded. This causes no integrability difficulty here: \(X\in L^2\) implies \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\in L^2\), so the residual is also square-integrable. With finitely many pricing groups, the premiums are bounded and the residual does have a constant lower bound.
The insurer bears within-group variance, while premium differences reflect between-group variance. With \(n\) independent copies of \((X,Y)\), the variance of the insurer’s average residual expenditure is
\[
\frac1n\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Y)].
\]
This separates the effect of conditional pricing from the effect of portfolio size.


A numerical illustration
Suppose half the population has a claim probability of \(1/10\) and half has a claim probability of \(3/10\). Every claim costs \(1{,}000\). Let \(Y\) identify the two groups. Their conditional means are \(100\) and \(300\), and their conditional variances are
\[
1{,}000^2\times\frac1{10}\times\frac9{10}=90{,}000
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
1{,}000^2\times\frac3{10}\times\frac7{10}=210{,}000.
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X]&=200,\\
\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Y)]&=150{,}000,\\
\text{and}\qquad\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Y])&=10{,}000.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence \(\mathbb V(X)=160{,}000\). Variances are expressed in squared currency units.
Under the common premium \(200\), the lower-risk group pays \(100\) more than its expected cost and the higher-risk group pays \(100\) less. Conditional pricing removes this average transfer between the two groups, but substantial uncertainty remains within each group. People with the same claim probability still do not all make the same claim.

title: Probability for insurance: risk pooling, segmentation and solidarity
section: Risk pooling and solidarity with incomplete segmentation
text:
Risk pooling and solidarity with incomplete segmentation

Used information and finer risk factors
The choice is rarely between no segmentation and a complete description of the risk. In the travel example, an insurer might use destination and duration to set the premium, while leaving activities out. Within a destination-and-duration group, the same distinction between mutualisation and solidarity would remain.
Let \(Y\) now denote the characteristics used for pricing, and let
\[
Z=(Y,\widetilde Y)
\]
include additional risk factors \(\widetilde Y\). These may be unobserved, difficult to measure, or deliberately excluded from pricing. The finer information \(Z\) provides a benchmark for expected cost; it need not capture every determinant of the loss.
For the travellers above, take \(Y\) to be constant because everyone has the same destination and duration, and let \(\widetilde Y\) describe their activity group. The insurer’s variance under the common premium then contains \(150{,}000\) of residual claim uncertainty and \(10{,}000\) of differences in expected cost left unpriced. We now express this distinction in general.
Since \(\sigma(Y)\subseteq\sigma(Z)\), the tower property gives
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[X\mid Z]\mid Y\right]=\mathbb E[X\mid Y].
\]
Under the premium \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\), the insurer’s expenditure decomposes as
\[
X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]
=\bigl(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Z]\bigr)
+\bigl(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\bigr).
\]
The two components have different meanings:

\(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Z]\) is residual claim uncertainty after accounting for the finer risk factors. Its conditional expectation given \(Z\) is zero. Sharing these fluctuations across many risks is the role of mutualisation.
\(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\) is a difference in expected cost left unpriced. When it is positive, the policyholder pays less than their finer conditional expected cost; when it is negative, they pay more. These expected transfers express solidarity, or cross-subsidisation, relative to the benchmark \(Z\).

The policyholder’s premium excess relative to that benchmark is the opposite quantity, \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]-\mathbb E[X\mid Z]\). The expected transfers balance within each pricing group:
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\mid Y\right]=0.
\]
However, for a finer risk profile, the insurer’s conditional expected expenditure is
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\mid Z\right]
=\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y].
\]
Thus the insurer can break even on average within a \(Y\)-group while expecting a surplus on some finer subgroups and a loss on others. Those expected surpluses finance the expected losses.


A three-part decomposition of variance

Proposition 5 (Refining the segmentation) Let \(X\in L^2\) and \(Z=(Y,\widetilde Y)\). Then
\[
\mathbb V(X\mid Y)
=\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Z)\mid Y]
+\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]\mid Y).
\]


Proof. Using the decomposition above, square and take the conditional expectation given \(Y\). The cross term vanishes: first conditioning on \(Z\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E\!\left[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Z])
(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])\mid Z\right]\\
&\qquad=(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])
\mathbb E[X-\mathbb E[X\mid Z]\mid Z]=0,
\end{aligned}
\]
and the tower property then gives zero after conditioning on \(Y\). The first squared term satisfies
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Z])^2\mid Y\right]
=\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Z)\mid Y].
\]
For the second, the tower property gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E\!\left[(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2\mid Y\right]\\
&\qquad=\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]\mid Y).
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding the two proves the identity.

Taking expectations yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Y)]
&=\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Z)]\\
&\quad+\mathbb E\!\left[(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining this with the law of total variance gives the three-part decomposition
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb V(X)
&=\underbrace{\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Z)]}_{\text{residual claim uncertainty}}\\[4pt]
&\quad+\underbrace{\mathbb E\!\left[(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2\right]}_{\text{unpriced differences in expected cost}}\\[4pt]
&\quad+\underbrace{\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Y])}_{\text{differences reflected in premiums}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The middle term can also be written as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\!\left[(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2\right]
&=\mathbb E[\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]\mid Y)]\\
&=\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Z])-\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]).
\end{aligned}
\]
It measures the dispersion of expected costs left unpriced by \(Y\). It is not the signed average transfer, which is zero, nor a measure of the social value of solidarity.
With pricing still based on \(Y\), the expenditure table can now distinguish the two sources of the insurer’s variance:

Variance of net expenditure

\(\mathbb E[X]\)
\(\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Y])\)


Insurer
\(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\)
\(0\)
\(\begin{gathered}\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Z)]\\{}+\mathbb E[(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2]\end{gathered}\)


Total

Pooling independent risks can make average expenditure more predictable. It does not remove the expected transfers between finer risk profiles: lower-expected-cost subgroups still finance higher-expected-cost subgroups within each pricing group. Dependence between claims and the composition of the portfolio remain relevant to the insurer’s aggregate risk.


Why not use every possible factor?
More information cannot increase the theoretical minimum mean squared prediction error:
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Z])^2\right]
\leq\mathbb E\!\left[(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y])^2\right].
\]
Equality holds exactly when \(\mathbb E[X\mid Z]=\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\) almost surely. This comparison assumes that the joint distribution is known and that we can compute its conditional expectations. In practice, these must be estimated from data. Adding variables does not guarantee better predictions on new observations: smaller groups and estimation error can offset the benefit of finer information.
Nor does better prediction settle which distinctions should determine premiums. Some characteristics are unobserved, unreliable or costly to obtain. Others may be deliberately excluded to protect privacy, preserve access to insurance or avoid distinctions considered unacceptable. Legal restrictions can also limit their use. Moreover, excluding a characteristic explicitly does not necessarily remove its influence if other variables act as proxies.
Genetic information makes the ethical issue particularly clear. DNA tests may reveal a predisposition to a disease before symptoms appear. Should that information affect insurance premiums? Someone might accept higher premiums for smokers, viewing smoking as behaviour that can be changed, yet reject higher premiums for people born with a genetic predisposition they did not choose. Even that distinction invites discussion: addiction and social circumstances complicate the idea of a freely chosen behaviour. Better knowledge of expected costs does not itself determine which differences people should be asked to bear.
Solidarity can be a deliberate response. A community may wish to share the expected costs of inherited illnesses, preserve broad access to cover, or maintain premiums that do not change with every new piece of personal information. Conversely, pricing and contract design may encourage prevention, and transfers between risk groups can affect willingness to participate in a common pool. These are ethical, social and economic choices. There is no mathematical identity that resolves them.
Finally, the distinction between heterogeneity and residual uncertainty depends on the information considered and on when it becomes available. Pricing characteristics must be available before the insured loss is realised; using the realised loss itself would defeat the purpose of insurance. Conditional expectation provides a precise language for distinguishing chance losses from differences in expected costs, while leaving the choice of pricing information open to statistical, economic and social judgement.

title: Chapter 4 — Insurance Pricing and Risk Measures
text:
The previous chapters introduced the pure premium: if the insurer’s random payment is \(X\), its pure premium is \(\mathbb E[X]\). When pricing uses observable characteristics, this expectation is taken under the conditional distribution of the claim given those characteristics. Throughout this chapter, the relevant information is understood to be fixed.
Charging the pure premium balances claims and premiums in expectation. It leaves no allowance for expenses, and no margin for adverse deviations from the expected claims. We therefore also considered premiums of the form
\[
\mathbb E[X]+c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(1+\theta)\mathbb E[X],
\]
where \(c\geq0\) and \(\theta\geq0\). These additive or multiplicative loadings can provide a first allowance for risk and expenses. For the mathematical discussion below, however, it is useful to distinguish expenses, which must be paid even if claims are perfectly predictable, from a safety loading, which compensates for bearing uncertainty.
A loading based only on the expectation cannot distinguish two risks with the same mean. Consider, for instance,
\[
X=100\quad\text{almost surely},
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb P(Y=10\,000)=0.01,\quad \mathbb P(Y=0)=0.99.
\]
Both have expectation \(100\), but \(\mathbb V(X)=0\) and \(\mathbb V(Y)=990\,000\). The same expected payment does not mean the same uncertainty. There is no reason to insist on the same safety loading when the risks have such different distributions.
A natural next attempt is
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\lambda\sqrt{\mathbb V(X)},
\qquad \lambda\geq0.
\]
This takes dispersion into account. But why use the standard deviation? Why not the variance, a utility function, or a feature of the upper tail? And how should the premium change when risks are combined?
These questions lead to premium principles: rules assigning a number \(\pi(X)\) to a random payment \(X\). We first study their mathematical properties, then return to the way premiums are actually assembled. This will lead us from individual contracts to the measurement of portfolio risk.


Initially, \(X\) denotes a nonnegative claim. A principle must be defined on an appropriate class of claims: integrable claims for the expectation, square-integrable claims for variance-based formulas, and sometimes a smaller class. Every statement below is understood whenever its arguments belong to the domain of the principle.
The following properties are natural candidates. They are a list of objectives to discuss, rather than a claim that every commercial premium must satisfy every one of them.

Law invariance. If \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same distribution, then \(\pi(X)=\pi(Y)\). A stand-alone principle uses the distribution of payments, not the labels attached to outcomes.
Normalisation and exact pricing of certain payments. We would like \(\pi(0)=0\) and \(\pi(c)=c\) for a deterministic payment \(c\geq0\). There is no uncertainty to remunerate. Explicit administrative expenses can be added separately.
Nonnegative safety loading. We would like
\[
\pi(X)\geq\mathbb E[X].
\]
Otherwise the expected underwriting result is negative even before expenses. Strict inequality for every nonconstant claim is a stronger requirement.
Monotonicity. If \(X\leq Y\) almost surely, then
\[
\pi(X)\leq\pi(Y).
\]
A contract that never pays more should not cost more under the same principle.
Cash additivity, also called translation equivariance. For a deterministic amount \(c\),
\[
\pi(X+c)=\pi(X)+c.
\]
Adding a certain payment changes the premium by that amount. Together with normalisation, this implies exact pricing of certain payments. For nonnegative claims, shifts must keep the claim in the domain; later, with real-valued losses, we allow all real shifts.
Positive homogeneity. For \(a\geq0\),
\[
\pi(aX)=a\pi(X).
\]
Scaling every payment by the same factor scales its premium accordingly. Here the parameter of the principle is held fixed.
Subadditivity. For two claims on the same probability space,
\[
\pi(X+Y)\leq\pi(X)+\pi(Y).
\]
Combining risks should not cost more than pricing them separately. This is a weak diversification requirement: it does not require a strict benefit, and it must take their dependence into account.
Convexity. For \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
\pi(\theta X+(1-\theta)Y)
\leq\theta\pi(X)+(1-\theta)\pi(Y).
\]
Mixing exposures should not increase the premium beyond the corresponding mixture of premiums. Positive homogeneity and subadditivity together imply convexity; with positive homogeneity, convexity conversely implies subadditivity.

Two further properties are useful. No unjustified loading asks that \(\pi(X)\leq\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\) for bounded claims. It follows from monotonicity and exact pricing of certain payments. Additivity for independent risks asks that \(\pi(X+Y)=\pi(X)+\pi(Y)\) when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent. Some classical principles satisfy it, although a principle intended to reward pooling may reasonably give a strict inequality instead.
One may also ask for continuity under a specified mode of convergence and for premiums to increase under a mean-preserving spread. These are meaningful additional requirements, but their precise formulation depends on the domain and on the topology being used.






NoteA premium is not just a list of axioms



A fixed administrative fee breaks normalisation. A percentage expense allowance can break cash additivity. A loading for concentration may break homogeneity. These observations do not make such commercial charges illegitimate. They explain why we should distinguish a mathematical rule for the risk component from the final price of a contract.





The simplest loaded principle is
\[
\pi(X)=(1+\theta)\mathbb E[X],\qquad \theta>0.
\]
It is monotone, positively homogeneous and additive, even for dependent risks. For nonnegative claims it has a nonnegative loading. However,
\[
\pi(X+c)=\pi(X)+(1+\theta)c,
\]
so it is not cash additive and charges a loading even on certain payments. It also gives exactly the same premium to every claim with the same expectation.
The pure premium, obtained with \(\theta=0\), satisfies all the principal algebraic properties above. Its limitation is economic: it contains no safety loading. Good axioms alone do not force a substantial margin for uncertainty.



For \(X\in L^2\), set
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\lambda\sqrt{\mathbb V(X)},\qquad\lambda>0.
\]
This principle is cash additive, positively homogeneous, exact on constants and larger than the expectation. It is also subadditive, because the triangle inequality in \(L^2\) gives
\[
\sqrt{\mathbb V(X+Y)}
=\left\|(X-\mathbb E[X])+(Y-\mathbb E[Y])\right\|_2
\leq\sqrt{\mathbb V(X)}+\sqrt{\mathbb V(Y)}.
\]
Consequently, it is convex. For independent nonconstant risks, the square root in the loading produces a strict pooling benefit.
Its defect is more surprising: it need not be monotone. Let \(X\) take values \(0\) and \(1\), with probabilities \(p\) and \(1-p\), and let \(Y=1\). Then \(X\leq Y\), but
\[
\pi(X)=1-p+\lambda\sqrt{p(1-p)}>1=\pi(Y)
\quad\text{if}\quad
0<p<\frac{\lambda^2}{1+\lambda^2}.
\]
For every \(\lambda>0\), such a \(p\) exists. The principle can charge more for a claim than its maximum possible payment. The problem is that increasing a payment in favourable states can reduce its standard deviation enough to reduce the premium.



Another classical choice is
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\lambda\mathbb V(X),\qquad\lambda>0.
\]
It is exact on constants, cash additive and has a nonnegative safety loading. Variance is convex as a functional on \(L^2\), so this principle is convex. It is also additive for independent risks, since
\[
\pi(X+Y)-\pi(X)-\pi(Y)=2\lambda\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).
\]
This identity displays the failure of general subadditivity: take \(Y=X\) with \(\mathbb V(X)>0\). Positive homogeneity fails as well:
\[
\pi(aX)=a\mathbb E[X]+\lambda a^2\mathbb V(X).
\]
The coefficient \(\lambda\) therefore has units of inverse currency. A change of currency requires a corresponding change in \(\lambda\); it is not homogeneity with a fixed parameter.
Monotonicity also fails. If \(X\) is \(0\) with probability \(p\) and \(a\) otherwise, whereas \(Y=a\), then
\[
\pi(X)-\pi(Y)=ap\bigl(\lambda a(1-p)-1\bigr)>0
\quad\text{when}\quad
\lambda a(1-p)>1.
\]
Thus, using a variance loading does not resolve the problem encountered with the standard deviation.



The microeconomic chapter suggests another approach. Let \(u\) be increasing and concave, and let \(w\) be initial wealth. The certainty equivalent of terminal wealth \(w-X\) is
\[
u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\right).
\]
The corresponding certainty-equivalent premium for full insurance is
\[
\pi_w(X)=w-u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\right).
\]
It solves
\[
u(w-\pi_w(X))=\mathbb E[u(w-X)].
\]
This is the largest premium that this policyholder would pay to replace the loss by a certain payment. Assume that terminal wealth remains in the domain of \(u\), that the expectation is finite, and that the inverse is well defined at that expectation.
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\leq u(w-\mathbb E[X]),
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
\pi_w(X)\geq\mathbb E[X].
\]
The rule is monotone and exact on constants. However, its other properties depend on the utility function, and it generally depends on initial wealth.
CARA utility. For \(u(z)=-e^{-\gamma z}\), with \(\gamma>0\), the dependence on wealth disappears:
\[
\pi(X)=\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}].
\]
This is the exponential premium principle, also called the entropic premium. It is finite when the required exponential moment exists. It is monotone, cash additive and convex, and it exceeds the expectation. Independence gives
\[
\mathbb E[e^{\gamma(X+Y)}]
=\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}]\mathbb E[e^{\gamma Y}],
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\pi(X+Y)=\pi(X)+\pi(Y).
\]
But it is not generally subadditive. For a bounded nonconstant \(X\), the strict positivity of \(\mathbb V(e^{\gamma X})\) yields
\[
\mathbb E[e^{2\gamma X}]>\bigl(\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}]\bigr)^2,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
\pi(2X)>2\pi(X).
\]
This also disproves positive homogeneity. Moreover, many heavy-tailed claims have no finite positive exponential moment.
For bounded \(X\), expansion as \(\gamma\) tends to zero gives
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\frac\gamma2\mathbb V(X)+O(\gamma^2).
\]
The variance principle can therefore be interpreted as a local approximation to an exponential premium.
CRRA utility. For relative risk aversion \(\eta>0\), use the traditional positive-wealth domain and write
\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{z^{1-\eta}}{1-\eta},&\eta\ne1,\\[4pt]
\log z,&\eta=1,
\end{cases}
\qquad z>0.
\]
When \(0<\eta<1\), the utility extends continuously to \(0\) with value \(0\). We keep terminal wealth strictly positive here to cover all parameters with the same formulas. For example, assume \(0\leq X\leq w-\varepsilon\) almost surely for some \(\varepsilon>0\). Then
\[
\pi_w(X)=
\begin{cases}
w-\left(\mathbb E[(w-X)^{1-\eta}]\right)^{1/(1-\eta)},&\eta\ne1,\\[4pt]
w-\exp\!\left(\mathbb E[\log(w-X)]\right),&\eta=1.
\end{cases}
\]
These premiums explicitly depend on wealth. They satisfy
\[
\pi_{aw}(aX)=a\pi_w(X),\qquad a>0,
\]
but this scales wealth and claims together. It does not give positive homogeneity of \(\pi_w\) at fixed wealth. Nor is \(\pi_w\) generally cash additive: changing a certain component of the loss also changes the wealth at which the remaining uncertainty is borne.
For a concrete illustration, let \(u=\log\), \(w=3\), and let \(X\) equal \(0\) or \(1\), each with probability \(1/2\). Then
\[
\pi_3(X)=3-\sqrt6,\qquad
\pi_3(X+1)=3-\sqrt2\ne\pi_3(X)+1,
\]
and
\[
\pi_3(2X)=3-\sqrt3>2(3-\sqrt6)=2\pi_3(X).
\]
The last inequality disproves both homogeneity and general subadditivity. Under CRRA utility the certainty equivalent of positive wealth is concave, so the corresponding loss premium is convex; convexity without homogeneity does not imply subadditivity.






NoteThe policyholder’s certainty equivalent and the insurer’s premium



The preceding certainty equivalent describes willingness to pay. An insurer with wealth \(w\) receiving a premium \(p\) instead uses the indifference equation
\[
\mathbb E[u(w+p-X)]=u(w).
\]
These are different equations. For CARA utility they give the same exponential premium. For CRRA utility the insurer’s premium is generally obtained by solving
\[
\mathbb E[(w+p-X)^{1-\eta}]=w^{1-\eta}
\quad\text{or}\quad
\mathbb E[\log(w+p-X)]=\log w,
\]
with positive terminal wealth. Unlike the policyholder’s certainty-equivalent premium at fixed wealth, this indifference premium is cash additive: replacing \(X\) by \(X+c\) replaces the solution \(p\) by \(p+c\). Keeping track of whose preferences are being used matters.

title: Probability for insurance: risk pooling, segmentation and solidarity
section: Who bears the expenditure? The case of pure-premium pricing
text:
Who bears the expenditure? The case of pure-premium pricing

The accounting convention
To keep the accounting simple, we consider full insurance of a nonnegative loss \(X\in L^2\), priced at the pure premium, with no expenses, loading, default or time discounting. We view \(X\) as the loss of a policyholder drawn from the population. The premium \(\pi\) is paid before the loss is realised and may depend on characteristics known at inception.
The policyholder incurs the loss \(X\), receives the indemnity \(X\), and pays \(\pi\). Their net expenditure is therefore \(\pi\). The insurer pays \(X\) and receives \(\pi\), so its net expenditure is \(X-\pi\). A negative insurer expenditure is a net receipt. Adding the two leaves the underlying loss \(X\).
Without insurance, the policyholder’s expenditure would be \(X\), with expectation \(\mathbb E[X]\) and variance \(\mathbb V(X)\).


A common pure premium: no segmentation
Charge everyone the same premium \(\pi=\mathbb E[X]\).









Party
Net expenditure
Expected net expenditure
Variance of net expenditure




Policyholder
\(\mathbb E[X]\)
\(\mathbb E[X]\)
\(0\)


Insurer
\(X-\mathbb E[X]\)
\(0\)
\(\mathbb V(X)\)


Total
\(X\)
\(\mathbb E[X]\)
\(\mathbb V(X)\)



The policyholder exchanges the uncertain loss for a constant payment. The insurer takes on all the variance associated with a randomly selected policy, while breaking even in expectation. Pooling many independent policies then reduces the variability of the insurer’s average net expenditure.


Segmentation using \(Y\)
Now charge the conditional pure premium
\[
\pi=\mathbb E[X\mid Y].
\]
The premium is constant within each group but can vary across groups. The table gives unconditional moments, before the group of the randomly selected policyholder is specified.









Party

Variance of net expenditure




Policyholder
\(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\)
