Here the variances add because the two expenditure variables are uncorrelated:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\mathbb E[X\mid Y],X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\right)=0.
\]
Variances do not add in general; the orthogonality of conditional expectation is doing the work.
For a policyholder whose group \(y\) is already known, the premium is the fixed amount \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y=y]\). Whatever claim occurs, full insurance reimburses it, leaving this same premium as the policyholder’s net expenditure. Its variance within that group is therefore zero. The policyholder variance in the table instead measures differences in premiums across the population. The insurer bears within-group uncertainty, while premium differences reflect between-group differences in expected costs.
Although \(X\geq0\), the residual \(X-\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\) may have no constant lower bound if premiums are unbounded. This causes no difficulty: both \(X\) and \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]\) belong to \(L^2\), so their difference does too.


A numerical illustration: travellers with different activities
Consider travellers visiting the same destination for the same duration. In a simplified model, half choose relatively quiet activities and have claim probability \(1/10\); the other half choose more hazardous activities and have claim probability \(3/10\). Every claim costs €1,000. Let \(Y\) identify the activity group.
The conditional expected costs are €100 and €300, and the conditional variances, in euros squared, are
\[
1{,}000^2\times\frac1{10}\times\frac9{10}=90{,}000
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
1{,}000^2\times\frac3{10}\times\frac7{10}=210{,}000.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[X]=200,\qquad
\mathbb E[\mathbb V(X\mid Y)]=150{,}000
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb V(\mathbb E[X\mid Y])=10{,}000.
\]
The total variance is therefore \(\mathbb V(X)=160{,}000\), in euros squared.
Under the common premium of €200, each quieter traveller pays €100 more than their expected cost, while each more adventurous traveller pays €100 less. This is solidarity between the two groups, whether or not the travellers intended these transfers. Meanwhile, within either group, some travellers make a claim and others do not. Sharing those chance losses is mutualisation.
Pricing by activity group removes the average transfer between the two groups. It does not remove the uncertainty within either group: the insurer still bears the within-group variance of \(150{,}000\). The remaining \(10{,}000\) appears as variance in premiums across policyholders.

title: Chapter 4 — Insurance Pricing and Risk Measures
text:
The previous chapters introduced the pure premium: if the insurer’s random payment is \(X\), its pure premium is \(\mathbb E[X]\). When pricing uses observable characteristics, this expectation is taken under the conditional distribution of the claim given those characteristics. Throughout this chapter, the relevant information is understood to be fixed.
Charging the pure premium balances claims and premiums in expectation. It leaves no allowance for expenses, and no margin for adverse deviations from the expected claims. We therefore also considered premiums of the form
\[
\mathbb E[X]+c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(1+\theta)\mathbb E[X],
\]
where \(c\geq0\) and \(\theta\geq0\). These additive or multiplicative loadings can provide a first allowance for risk and expenses. For the mathematical discussion below, however, it is useful to distinguish expenses, which must be paid even if claims are perfectly predictable, from a safety loading, which compensates for bearing uncertainty.
A loading based only on the expectation cannot distinguish two risks with the same mean. Consider, for instance,
\[
X=100\quad\text{almost surely},
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb P(Y=10\,000)=0.01,\quad \mathbb P(Y=0)=0.99.
\]
Both have expectation \(100\), but \(\mathbb V(X)=0\) and \(\mathbb V(Y)=990\,000\). The same expected payment does not mean the same uncertainty. There is no reason to insist on the same safety loading when the risks have such different distributions.
A natural next attempt is
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\lambda\sqrt{\mathbb V(X)},
\qquad \lambda\geq0.
\]
This takes dispersion into account. But why use the standard deviation? Why not the variance, a utility function, or a feature of the upper tail? And how should the premium change when risks are combined?
These questions lead to premium principles: rules assigning a number \(\pi(X)\) to a random payment \(X\). We first study their mathematical properties, then return to the way premiums are actually assembled. This will lead us from individual contracts to the measurement of portfolio risk.


Initially, \(X\) denotes a nonnegative claim. A principle must be defined on an appropriate class of claims: integrable claims for the expectation, square-integrable claims for variance-based formulas, and sometimes a smaller class. Every statement below is understood whenever its arguments belong to the domain of the principle.
The following properties are natural candidates. They are a list of objectives to discuss, rather than a claim that every commercial premium must satisfy every one of them.

Law invariance. If \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same distribution, then \(\pi(X)=\pi(Y)\). A stand-alone principle uses the distribution of payments, not the labels attached to outcomes.
Normalisation and exact pricing of certain payments. We would like \(\pi(0)=0\) and \(\pi(c)=c\) for a deterministic payment \(c\geq0\). There is no uncertainty to remunerate. Explicit administrative expenses can be added separately.
Nonnegative safety loading. We would like
\[
\pi(X)\geq\mathbb E[X].
\]
Otherwise the expected underwriting result is negative even before expenses. Strict inequality for every nonconstant claim is a stronger requirement.
Monotonicity. If \(X\leq Y\) almost surely, then
\[
\pi(X)\leq\pi(Y).
\]
A contract that never pays more should not cost more under the same principle.
Cash additivity, also called translation equivariance. For a deterministic amount \(c\),
\[
\pi(X+c)=\pi(X)+c.
\]
Adding a certain payment changes the premium by that amount. Together with normalisation, this implies exact pricing of certain payments. For nonnegative claims, shifts must keep the claim in the domain; later, with real-valued losses, we allow all real shifts.
Positive homogeneity. For \(a\geq0\),
\[
\pi(aX)=a\pi(X).
\]
Scaling every payment by the same factor scales its premium accordingly. Here the parameter of the principle is held fixed.
Subadditivity. For two claims on the same probability space,
\[
\pi(X+Y)\leq\pi(X)+\pi(Y).
\]
Combining risks should not cost more than pricing them separately. This is a weak diversification requirement: it does not require a strict benefit, and it must take their dependence into account.
Convexity. For \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
\pi(\theta X+(1-\theta)Y)
\leq\theta\pi(X)+(1-\theta)\pi(Y).
\]
Mixing exposures should not increase the premium beyond the corresponding mixture of premiums. Positive homogeneity and subadditivity together imply convexity; with positive homogeneity, convexity conversely implies subadditivity.

Two further properties are useful. No unjustified loading asks that \(\pi(X)\leq\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\) for bounded claims. It follows from monotonicity and exact pricing of certain payments. Additivity for independent risks asks that \(\pi(X+Y)=\pi(X)+\pi(Y)\) when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent. Some classical principles satisfy it, although a principle intended to reward pooling may reasonably give a strict inequality instead.
One may also ask for continuity under a specified mode of convergence and for premiums to increase under a mean-preserving spread. These are meaningful additional requirements, but their precise formulation depends on the domain and on the topology being used.






NoteA premium is not just a list of axioms



A fixed administrative fee breaks normalisation. A percentage expense allowance can break cash additivity. A loading for concentration may break homogeneity. These observations do not make such commercial charges illegitimate. They explain why we should distinguish a mathematical rule for the risk component from the final price of a contract.





The simplest loaded principle is
\[
\pi(X)=(1+\theta)\mathbb E[X],\qquad \theta>0.
\]
It is monotone, positively homogeneous and additive, even for dependent risks. For nonnegative claims it has a nonnegative loading. However,
\[
\pi(X+c)=\pi(X)+(1+\theta)c,
\]
so it is not cash additive and charges a loading even on certain payments. It also gives exactly the same premium to every claim with the same expectation.
The pure premium, obtained with \(\theta=0\), satisfies all the principal algebraic properties above. Its limitation is economic: it contains no safety loading. Good axioms alone do not force a substantial margin for uncertainty.



For \(X\in L^2\), set
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\lambda\sqrt{\mathbb V(X)},\qquad\lambda>0.
\]
This principle is cash additive, positively homogeneous, exact on constants and larger than the expectation. It is also subadditive, because the triangle inequality in \(L^2\) gives
\[
\sqrt{\mathbb V(X+Y)}
=\left\|(X-\mathbb E[X])+(Y-\mathbb E[Y])\right\|_2
\leq\sqrt{\mathbb V(X)}+\sqrt{\mathbb V(Y)}.
\]
Consequently, it is convex. For independent nonconstant risks, the square root in the loading produces a strict pooling benefit.
Its defect is more surprising: it need not be monotone. Let \(X\) take values \(0\) and \(1\), with probabilities \(p\) and \(1-p\), and let \(Y=1\). Then \(X\leq Y\), but
\[
\pi(X)=1-p+\lambda\sqrt{p(1-p)}>1=\pi(Y)
\quad\text{if}\quad
0<p<\frac{\lambda^2}{1+\lambda^2}.
\]
For every \(\lambda>0\), such a \(p\) exists. The principle can charge more for a claim than its maximum possible payment. The problem is that increasing a payment in favourable states can reduce its standard deviation enough to reduce the premium.



Another classical choice is
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\lambda\mathbb V(X),\qquad\lambda>0.
\]
It is exact on constants, cash additive and has a nonnegative safety loading. Variance is convex as a functional on \(L^2\), so this principle is convex. It is also additive for independent risks, since
\[
\pi(X+Y)-\pi(X)-\pi(Y)=2\lambda\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).
\]
This identity displays the failure of general subadditivity: take \(Y=X\) with \(\mathbb V(X)>0\). Positive homogeneity fails as well:
\[
\pi(aX)=a\mathbb E[X]+\lambda a^2\mathbb V(X).
\]
The coefficient \(\lambda\) therefore has units of inverse currency. A change of currency requires a corresponding change in \(\lambda\); it is not homogeneity with a fixed parameter.
Monotonicity also fails. If \(X\) is \(0\) with probability \(p\) and \(a\) otherwise, whereas \(Y=a\), then
\[
\pi(X)-\pi(Y)=ap\bigl(\lambda a(1-p)-1\bigr)>0
\quad\text{when}\quad
\lambda a(1-p)>1.
\]
Thus, using a variance loading does not resolve the problem encountered with the standard deviation.



The microeconomic chapter suggests another approach. Let \(u\) be increasing and concave, and let \(w\) be initial wealth. The certainty equivalent of terminal wealth \(w-X\) is
\[
u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\right).
\]
The corresponding certainty-equivalent premium for full insurance is
\[
\pi_w(X)=w-u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\right).
\]
It solves
\[
u(w-\pi_w(X))=\mathbb E[u(w-X)].
\]
This is the largest premium that this policyholder would pay to replace the loss by a certain payment. Assume that terminal wealth remains in the domain of \(u\), that the expectation is finite, and that the inverse is well defined at that expectation.
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\leq u(w-\mathbb E[X]),
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
\pi_w(X)\geq\mathbb E[X].
\]
The rule is monotone and exact on constants. However, its other properties depend on the utility function, and it generally depends on initial wealth.
CARA utility. For \(u(z)=-e^{-\gamma z}\), with \(\gamma>0\), the dependence on wealth disappears:
\[
\pi(X)=\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}].
\]
This is the exponential premium principle, also called the entropic premium. It is finite when the required exponential moment exists. It is monotone, cash additive and convex, and it exceeds the expectation. Independence gives
\[
\mathbb E[e^{\gamma(X+Y)}]
=\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}]\mathbb E[e^{\gamma Y}],
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\pi(X+Y)=\pi(X)+\pi(Y).
\]
But it is not generally subadditive. For a bounded nonconstant \(X\), the strict positivity of \(\mathbb V(e^{\gamma X})\) yields
\[
\mathbb E[e^{2\gamma X}]>\bigl(\mathbb E[e^{\gamma X}]\bigr)^2,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
\pi(2X)>2\pi(X).
\]
This also disproves positive homogeneity. Moreover, many heavy-tailed claims have no finite positive exponential moment.
For bounded \(X\), expansion as \(\gamma\) tends to zero gives
\[
\pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\frac\gamma2\mathbb V(X)+O(\gamma^2).
\]
The variance principle can therefore be interpreted as a local approximation to an exponential premium.
CRRA utility. For relative risk aversion \(\eta>0\), use the traditional positive-wealth domain and write
\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{z^{1-\eta}}{1-\eta},&\eta\ne1,\\[4pt]
\log z,&\eta=1,
\end{cases}
\qquad z>0.
\]
When \(0<\eta<1\), the utility extends continuously to \(0\) with value \(0\). We keep terminal wealth strictly positive here to cover all parameters with the same formulas. For example, assume \(0\leq X\leq w-\varepsilon\) almost surely for some \(\varepsilon>0\). Then
\[
\pi_w(X)=
\begin{cases}
w-\left(\mathbb E[(w-X)^{1-\eta}]\right)^{1/(1-\eta)},&\eta\ne1,\\[4pt]
w-\exp\!\left(\mathbb E[\log(w-X)]\right),&\eta=1.
\end{cases}
\]
These premiums explicitly depend on wealth. They satisfy
\[
\pi_{aw}(aX)=a\pi_w(X),\qquad a>0,
\]
but this scales wealth and claims together. It does not give positive homogeneity of \(\pi_w\) at fixed wealth. Nor is \(\pi_w\) generally cash additive: changing a certain component of the loss also changes the wealth at which the remaining uncertainty is borne.
For a concrete illustration, let \(u=\log\), \(w=3\), and let \(X\) equal \(0\) or \(1\), each with probability \(1/2\). Then
\[
\pi_3(X)=3-\sqrt6,\qquad
\pi_3(X+1)=3-\sqrt2\ne\pi_3(X)+1,
\]
and
\[
\pi_3(2X)=3-\sqrt3>2(3-\sqrt6)=2\pi_3(X).
\]
The last inequality disproves both homogeneity and general subadditivity. Under CRRA utility the certainty equivalent of positive wealth is concave, so the corresponding loss premium is convex; convexity without homogeneity does not imply subadditivity.






NoteThe policyholder’s certainty equivalent and the insurer’s premium



The preceding certainty equivalent describes willingness to pay. An insurer with wealth \(w\) receiving a premium \(p\) instead uses the indifference equation
\[
\mathbb E[u(w+p-X)]=u(w).
\]
These are different equations. For CARA utility they give the same exponential premium. For CRRA utility the insurer’s premium is generally obtained by solving
\[
\mathbb E[(w+p-X)^{1-\eta}]=w^{1-\eta}
\quad\text{or}\quad

\]

title: Chapter 4 — Insurance Pricing and Risk Measures
text:
A detour through pricing practice

A premium is assembled from several ingredients
In practice, insurers combine statistical estimates, expense allowances, reinsurance costs, capital costs and commercial adjustments. The resulting tariff rarely follows one universal formula \(\pi(X)\) applied mechanically to every individual contract.
A simple illustrative calculation starts from expected annual claims \(m\). Suppose there are fixed expenses \(e\), proportional expenses equal to a fraction \(a<1\) of the premium, and a monetary allowance \(k\) for the cost of bearing risk. Balancing the amounts gives
\[
p=m+e+ap+k,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
p=\frac{m+e+k}{1-a}.
\]
For \(m=300\), \(e=40\), \(k=20\), and \(a=0.20\), the indicated premium is \(450\). This example is before any separate taxes and assumes no investment income. The allowance \(k\) is a cost or required remuneration over the pricing period, not the entire amount of capital held by the insurer.
The expected claims themselves may be estimated by combining claim frequency and severity, or by modelling aggregate claims directly. In a simple compound model with an independent claim count and i.i.d. severities,
\[
\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[N]\mathbb E[Z_1].
\]
Risk characteristics, deductibles, limits, claims inflation and the development of claims not yet fully settled all affect this estimate. Sparse experience may be blended with broader experience. The commercial price may then be adjusted for distribution arrangements, competitive conditions and constraints on the tariff.
For a practical introduction, see Werner and Modlin’s Basic Ratemaking. The relevant lesson here is the distinction between a modelled claim cost, an allowance for expenses and capital, and a final selling price.


The risk belongs to the portfolio
Suppose the insurer already faces an aggregate loss \(S\) and is considering a new contract with loss \(X\). The additional risk depends on the joint distribution of \((S,X)\), not only on the distribution of \(X\). Even for variance,
\[
\mathbb V(S+X)-\mathbb V(S)=\mathbb V(X)+2\operatorname{Cov}(S,X).
\]
Two contracts with identical stand-alone distributions may make very different contributions to the insurer’s risk. A household policy that shares a flood exposure with thousands of existing policies is not equivalent, for the insurer, to an otherwise similar policy in a different region.
If \(K(S)\) denotes a portfolio capital requirement, an incremental approach may examine
\[
K(S+X)-K(S).
\]
A pricing allowance might remunerate this additional capital over the contract period. Other approaches allocate the total capital among contracts or business lines. The allocation problem is separate from the definition of the total requirement.
This is why risk measures become central. We now want a numerical assessment of an aggregate loss, for risk limits, capital allocation or solvency assessment. This is a general risk-management question, relevant in banking as well as insurance.


Loss measures and capital requirements
We use the loss convention: larger values of \(X\) are worse. Losses may now be real-valued, since a portfolio can make gains as well as losses. All amounts are expressed at a common horizon and in a common monetary unit.
A risk measure \(\rho(X)\) gives a monetary assessment of the loss. It should not automatically be read as additional capital on top of resources already available. If a deterministic amount \(b\) has already been provided and \(\rho\) is cash additive, then
\[
\rho(X-b)=\rho(X)-b.
\]
For example, in a simplified model that has already provided \(\mathbb E[X]\) for expected claims, the additional buffer suggested by \(\rho\) is \(\rho(X)-\mathbb E[X]\), subject to any nonnegativity constraint on capital. A full balance-sheet model contains many other items and risks.
This distinction also matters in regulation. Article 101 of Solvency II calibrates the Solvency Capital Requirement to a 99.5% Value-at-Risk standard over one year, in relation to basic own funds. It covers the undertaking’s risks, rather than defining the premium of each insurance policy. The standard formula or an approved internal model implements this framework; the formula for the quantile of an individual claim is not, by itself, a regulatory capital calculation.

title: Chapter 4 — Insurance Pricing and Risk Measures
text:
Value-at-Risk: a loss threshold

Definition and the role of the quantile convention
Let \(X\) be an almost surely finite real-valued loss, with cumulative distribution function
\[
F_X(x)=\mathbb P(X\leq x).
\]
For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)
=F_X^{-1}(\alpha)
=\inf\{x\in\mathbb R:F_X(x)\geq\alpha\}.
\]
No moment assumption is needed. This quantile is finite for every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).
Writing \(q=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\), the defining inequalities are
\[
F_X(q-)\leq\alpha\leq F_X(q),
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\mathbb P(X<q)\leq\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb P(X\leq q)\geq\alpha.
\]
In particular, \(\mathbb P(X>q)\leq1-\alpha\). These inequalities are essential when there are atoms. The equation \(F_X(q)=\alpha\) is not a general definition of a quantile.

Three quantile configurations: a standard normal distribution, a discrete distribution with a jump, and an equal mixture of uniform distributions on [0, 1] and [2, 3]. The dotted vertical line marks the lower quantile in each panel. Open circles exclude endpoints; filled circles include them.

For a continuous and strictly increasing CDF, the quantile is the unique solution of \(F_X(q)=\alpha\). At a jump, the horizontal level \(\alpha\) can lie strictly between \(F_X(q-)\) and \(F_X(q)\). On a plateau at height \(\alpha\), several values solve \(F_X(x)=\alpha\); our definition selects the left endpoint. Thus continuity of the CDF alone does not ensure a unique solution to that equation.


Properties of Value-at-Risk

Proposition 1 (Basic properties) For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), Value-at-Risk is law invariant, monotone, cash additive and positively homogeneous. It is exact on constants. More explicitly,
\[
X\leq Y\text{ almost surely}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\leq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y),
\]
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X+c)=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)+c,
\qquad c\in\mathbb R,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(aX)=a\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X),
\qquad a\geq0.
\]
Moreover, \(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\) is nondecreasing in \(\alpha\).

Proof. Law invariance follows from the definition. If \(X\leq Y\), then \(F_X(x)\geq F_Y(x)\) for every \(x\), so the first CDF reaches a given level no later than the second. For shifts, use \(F_{X+c}(x)=F_X(x-c)\). For \(a>0\), use \(F_{aX}(x)=F_X(x/a)\); the case \(a=0\) follows directly. A constant \(c\) has every quantile equal to \(c\). Finally, increasing the probability level can only move the first crossing to the right. \(\square\)
These are attractive properties. However, VaR need not dominate the expectation, and one major aggregation property is missing: VaR is not subadditive in general.


First counterexample: independent heavy-tailed losses
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent, with common density
\[
f(x)=\frac{\mathbf 1_{\{x\geq0\}}}{(1+x)^2}.
\]
For \(x\geq0\),
\[
\mathbb P(X>x)=\frac1{1+x},
\qquad
F_X(x)=\frac{x}{1+x},
\qquad
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}.
\]
We calculate the upper tail of the sum. For \(s\geq0\), conditioning on \(X\) gives
\[
\mathbb P(X+Y>s)
=\frac1{1+s}+\int_0^s\frac{\mathrm dx}{(1+x)^2(1+s-x)}.
\]
The first term corresponds to \(X>s\). For the integral, use the partial fraction decomposition
\[
\frac1{(1+x)^2(1+s-x)}
=\frac1{(s+2)^2}\left(\frac1{1+x}+\frac1{1+s-x}\right)
+\frac1{s+2}\frac1{(1+x)^2}.
\]
It follows that
\[
\int_0^s\frac{\mathrm dx}{(1+x)^2(1+s-x)}
=\frac{2\log(1+s)}{(s+2)^2}
+\frac1{s+2}\left(1-\frac1{1+s}\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\mathbb P(X+Y>s)
=\frac2{s+2}+\frac{2\log(1+s)}{(s+2)^2}.
\]
Set \(q=\alpha/(1-\alpha)>0\). At the sum of the individual quantiles,
\[
\mathbb P(X+Y>2q)
=\frac1{1+q}+\frac{\log(1+2q)}{2(1+q)^2}
>1-\alpha.
\]
The CDF of \(X+Y\) is continuous and strictly increasing on \((0,+\infty)\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X+Y)
>2q
=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)+\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y).
\]
This works for every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), despite independence.
These particular losses have infinite expectation, since \(\int_0^{+\infty}(1+x)^{-1}\,\mathrm dx=+\infty\). They illustrate a failure of VaR on its natural domain, but will not belong to the integrable domain used for ES below. The next example shows that the failure persists for bounded losses.


Second counterexample: credit insurance
Consider two credit insurance contracts with joint losses

Each contract pays nothing with probability \(96\%\). Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(X)=\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(Y)=0.
\]
Their sum is \(0\) with probability \(92\%\) and \(100\) with probability \(8\%\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(X+Y)=100>0+0.
\]
The losses here are dependent: their positive payments are mutually exclusive. There is no conflict with the independence assumption in the preceding example; these are two separate demonstrations.


What the threshold does not tell us
VaR answers a threshold question. It does not describe the severity of losses beyond that threshold. For example, if a loss is zero with probability \(96\%\) and equals \(M>0\) otherwise, its 95% VaR is zero for every value of \(M\).
In the credit example, each individual probability of loss lies below the 5% tail budget. The union of the two loss events does not. This abrupt change is a feature of threshold measurement, rather than evidence that combining these contracts has created an additional loss scenario.
The issue motivates a search for risk measures with better aggregation properties and a more explicit account of the upper tail.

title: Chapter 4 — Insurance Pricing and Risk Measures
text:
Coherent risk measures
The influential paper by Artzner, Delbaen, Eber and Heath, Coherent Measures of Risk (1999), proposed four axioms for monetary risk measurement. An author-hosted version is also available.
The subject was closely connected to practical risk management. Jean-Marc Eber’s affiliation on the paper was Société Générale, Paris. In the anecdote related by the lecturer, Eber had encountered failures of VaR subadditivity in actual banking data. The point of this anecdote is that aggregation problems were not merely a mathematical curiosity: controls applied to individual positions could give a misleading impression of the risk of their sum.


Definition 1 (Coherent risk measure: loss convention) On a linear space of losses, a finite-valued risk measure \(\rho\) is coherent if it satisfies:

Monotonicity: \(X\leq Y\) almost surely implies \(\rho(X)\leq\rho(Y)\).
Cash additivity: \(\rho(X+c)=\rho(X)+c\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R\).
Positive homogeneity: \(\rho(aX)=a\rho(X)\) for every \(a\geq0\).
Subadditivity: \(\rho(X+Y)\leq\rho(X)+\rho(Y)\).


These are very close to properties already considered for premium principles. Homogeneity gives \(\rho(0)=0\), cash additivity then gives \(\rho(c)=c\), and homogeneity together with subadditivity gives convexity. Law invariance is an additional property, not one of the four coherence axioms. A requirement such as \(\rho(X)\geq\mathbb E[X]\) is also not part of this definition.
The sign convention matters. If one uses future profit or wealth instead of losses, more money makes the position safer, and the signs in monotonicity and cash additivity change accordingly. Here we consistently work with losses.
VaR satisfies three of these four axioms but fails subadditivity. Can we retain a monetary interpretation while accounting for the losses in the upper tail?

title: Chapter 4 — Insurance Pricing and Risk Measures
section: Expected Shortfall: averaging the upper tail
text:
Expected Shortfall: averaging the upper tail

Why a conditional expectation is not the right starting definition
A tempting candidate is
\[
\mathbb E[X\mid X\geq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)].
\]
But why use \(\geq\) rather than \(>\)? If the distribution has an atom at the quantile, these conditions select different amounts of probability. Neither need select exactly \(1-\alpha\).
Take the individual credit loss above. At level \(95\%\), the quantile is zero, so
\[
\mathbb E[X\mid X\geq0]=4,
\qquad\text{whereas}\qquad
\mathbb E[X\mid X>0]=100.
\]
The first averages the whole population of outcomes; the second averages only 4% of it. To average the worst 5%, we need all the positive losses and one further percentage point of zero losses. The correct answer will be \(80\).
There is another difficulty with the strict inequality: the event can have probability zero, for instance for a constant loss. We therefore begin with a definition that handles continuous and discrete distributions uniformly.


Definition by integrated quantiles
From now on, assume \(X\in L^1\), unless explicitly stated otherwise. For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define the Expected Shortfall at level \(\alpha\) by
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
=\frac1{1-\alpha}\int_{\alpha}^1\operatorname{VaR}_{u}(X)\,\mathrm du.
\]
The value at the endpoint \(u=1\) does not affect the integral. Since
\[
\int_0^1\left|F_X^{-1}(u)\right|\,\mathrm du=\mathbb E[|X|],
\]
ES is finite on \(L^1\). It is the average of the upper \(1-\alpha\) fraction of quantiles. In particular,
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)\geq\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)\geq\mathbb E[X].
\]
The second inequality follows because the average of an increasing function over its upper interval is at least its average over the whole interval.


The stop-loss formula and the atom at the quantile

Proposition 2 (Two useful formulas) Let \(X\in L^1\), \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and \(q=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\). Then
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
=q+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-q)_+].}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
=\frac{\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{X>q\}}]
+q\bigl(F_X(q)-\alpha\bigr)}{1-\alpha}.}
\]

Proof. Write \(Q(u)=F_X^{-1}(u)\). For \(u<\alpha\), \(Q(u)\leq q\); for \(u>\alpha\), \(Q(u)\geq q\). Since \(Q(U)\) has the same distribution as \(X\) when \(U\) is uniform on \((0,1)\),
\[
\mathbb E[(X-q)_+]
=\int_0^1(Q(u)-q)_+\,\mathrm du
=\int_{\alpha}^1(Q(u)-q)\,\mathrm du.
\]
Rearranging proves the first formula. For the second, expand
\[
\mathbb E[(X-q)_+]
=\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{X>q\}}]-q\mathbb P(X>q)
\]
and use \(\mathbb P(X>q)=1-F_X(q)\). \(\square\)
The quantity \(\mathbb E[(X-q)_+]\) is a stop-loss premium, or the undiscounted expected payoff of a call on \(X\) with strike \(q\). Thus ES equals the VaR threshold plus the mean excess above that threshold, divided by the tail probability budget.
The second formula tells us precisely how to treat atoms. We include every outcome with \(X>q\), whose total probability is \(1-F_X(q)\), and add probability mass \(F_X(q)-\alpha\) from the outcomes with \(X=q\). This is possible because
\[
0\leq F_X(q)-\alpha\leq F_X(q)-F_X(q-)=\mathbb P(X=q).
\]
If the CDF is continuous at \(q\), then \(F_X(q)=\alpha\) and \(\mathbb P(X=q)=0\). In that case,
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)=\mathbb E[X\mid X>q]
=\mathbb E[X\mid X\geq q].
\]
Without that condition, the atom correction must be retained.
For the credit example,
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{0.95}(X)=\operatorname{ES}_{0.95}(Y)
=\frac{0.04\times100}{0.05}=80,
\]
whereas the sum has \(q=100\) and
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{0.95}(X+Y)=100.
\]
The desired aggregation inequality now holds: \(100\leq80+80\).

title: Chapter 4 — Insurance Pricing and Risk Measures
section: ES as a worst-case stress test
text:
ES as a worst-case stress test

Selecting events of exactly the right probability
To interpret ES as an average over an event of probability \(1-\alpha\), we must be able to select a fraction of a quantile atom. A finite probability space may not allow this. We therefore assume in this section that the space supports a uniform random variable on \((0,1)\).
This assumption allows every event to be divided into pieces of any desired smaller probability. Indeed, if \(U\) is uniform and \(A\) is an event, the function
\[
g(s)=\mathbb P(A\cap\{U\leq s\}),\qquad s\in[0,1],
\]
is continuous, because
\[
0\leq g(t)-g(s)\leq\mathbb P(s<U\leq t)=t-s,
\qquad 0\leq s\leq t\leq1.
\]
It ranges from \(0\) to \(\mathbb P(A)\). The intermediate value theorem gives the required subset. Notice that independence between \(U\) and \(A\) is not needed.
If necessary, we can enlarge the original space by taking its product with \((0,1)\) equipped with Lebesgue measure. Existing losses retain their joint distribution, and the additional coordinate supplies a uniform random variable. This does not change their VaR or ES.

Proposition 3 (Worst-event representation) On such a space, for every \(X\in L^1\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\),
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
=\frac1{1-\alpha}\sup_{\substack{B\in\mathcal F\\\mathbb P(B)=1-\alpha}}
\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_B].}
\]
The supremum is attained.

Proof. Let \(q=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\). Select an event \(A\subseteq\{X=q\}\) with probability \(F_X(q)-\alpha\), and set
\[
B^*=\{X>q\}\cup A.
\]
Then \(\mathbb P(B^*)=1-\alpha\), and the atom formula gives
\[
\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{B^*}]=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X).
\]
For any other event \(B\) of the same probability,
\[
(X-q)(\mathbf 1_{B^*}-\mathbf 1_B)\geq0
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
To see this, separate the cases \(X>q\), \(X<q\), and \(X=q\). The first factor and the difference of indicators have compatible signs in the first two cases, and the product vanishes in the third. Taking expectations and using equal probabilities gives
\[
\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{B^*}]-\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_B]
=\mathbb E[(X-q)(\mathbf 1_{B^*}-\mathbf 1_B)]\geq0.
\]
This proves the result. Integrability is enough; boundedness is not required. \(\square\)


Interpretation and coherence
Since every admissible \(B\) has probability \(1-\alpha\), the representation can also be written
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
=\sup_{\mathbb P(B)=1-\alpha}\mathbb E[X\mid B].
\]
We consider every stress event with a prescribed probability budget and retain the largest conditional mean loss. The worst event selects the largest losses, splitting the quantile atom if necessary. This is a mathematical stress-test interpretation; practical stress scenarios are often chosen in other ways and need not come with a reliable probability.
It also makes subadditivity transparent. For any admissible event \(B\),
\[
\mathbb E[(X+Y)\mathbf 1_B]
\leq\sup_{\mathbb P(A)=1-\alpha}\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_A]
+\sup_{\mathbb P(C)=1-\alpha}\mathbb E[Y\mathbf 1_C].
\]
Taking the supremum over \(B\) and dividing by \(1-\alpha\) gives
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X+Y)
\leq\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)+\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(Y).
\]
The worst event for the sum need not be the worst event for each component. That is exactly why the supremum of the sum is at most the sum of the suprema.
Monotonicity, cash additivity and positive homogeneity follow from the same representation, or directly from the quantile definition. Thus ES is a law-invariant coherent risk measure on \(L^1\). On an arbitrary original space, apply the argument after the common product enlargement; the distributions of \(X\), \(Y\) and \(X+Y\) are unchanged.

title: Chapter 4 — Insurance Pricing and Risk Measures
section: ES as a minimum: the Rockafellar–Uryasev formula
text:
ES as a minimum: the Rockafellar–Uryasev formula
There is another representation, with a different interpretation and particularly useful computational consequences. Fix \(X\in L^1\), \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and define
\[
f(t)=t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+],\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
\]
We already know that \(f(q)=\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)\) at \(q=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\). The stronger statement is that this value is the minimum over every possible threshold.

Theorem 1 (Variational representation) For \(X\in L^1\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\),
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)
=\min_{t\in\mathbb R}\left\{t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]\right\},}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\in
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{t\in\mathbb R}f(t).}
\]

Proof. Set \(t_0=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\). For any real \(t\), the pointwise identity
\[
(X-t)_+-(X-t_0)_+
=-\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathbf 1_{\{X>s\}}\,\mathrm ds
\]
holds, with the usual orientation of an integral when \(t<t_0\). The integral is over a finite interval with a bounded integrand, so we may interchange expectation and integration. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(t)-f(t_0)
&=t-t_0-\frac1{1-\alpha}\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathbb P(X>s)\,\mathrm ds\\
&=\frac1{1-\alpha}\int_{t_0}^{t}\bigl(F_X(s)-\alpha\bigr)\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(t\geq t_0\), then \(F_X(s)\geq\alpha\) for \(s\geq t_0\), and the integral is nonnegative. If \(t<t_0\), then \(F_X(s)<\alpha\) for \(s<t_0\), but the orientation of the integral is reversed, so it is again nonnegative. Therefore \(f(t)\geq f(t_0)\) for every \(t\). The stop-loss formula identifies \(f(t_0)\) as ES. \(\square\)
No density or differentiability of the CDF has been assumed. The proof covers both atoms and plateaux.

A minimum value and a minimising threshold
The two boxes describe different objects: ES is the minimum value; VaR is a minimising argument. The minimiser need not be unique. In fact,
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{t\in\mathbb R}f(t)
=\{t\in\mathbb R:F_X(t-)\leq\alpha\leq F_X(t)\}.
\]
For example, the one-sided derivatives of the convex function \(f\) are
\[
f'_-(t)=\frac{F_X(t-)-\alpha}{1-\alpha},
\qquad
f'_+(t)=\frac{F_X(t)-\alpha}{1-\alpha}.
\]
The minimum condition is \(f'_-(t)\leq0\leq f'_+(t)\). If the CDF has a plateau at height \(\alpha\), the corresponding interval consists of minimisers, whereas our VaR convention selects its left endpoint.
This should recall the least-squares characterisation from the previous chapter. For \(X\in L^2\),
\[
\mathbb V(X)=\min_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[(X-t)^2],
\qquad
\{\mathbb E[X]\}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[(X-t)^2],
\]
where the minimiser is unique. The parallel is between an optimal value and an optimal location:








Objective
Minimum value
Minimising location




\(\mathbb E[(X-t)^2]\)
\(\mathbb V(X)\)
\(\mathbb E[X]\), uniquely


\(t+(1-\alpha)^{-1}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]\)
\(\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)\)
\(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\), possibly among others



This is an analogy between optimisation characterisations; it does not identify ES with a dispersion measure. In particular, ES is cash additive, whereas variance is unchanged by a deterministic shift.


A second proof of subadditivity
Let \(q_X=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)\) and \(q_Y=\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(Y)\). The minimum representation and the inequality \((a+b)_+\leq a_++b_+\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X+Y)
&\leq q_X+q_Y+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X+Y-q_X-q_Y)_+]\\
&\leq q_X+q_Y+\frac1{1-\alpha}\left(\mathbb E[(X-q_X)_+]+\mathbb E[(Y-q_Y)_+]\right)\\
&=\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)+\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(Y).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proof works directly on the original probability space and requires no atom-splitting construction.
For further perspectives, see Embrechts and Wang, Seven Proofs for the Subadditivity of Expected Shortfall (2015), Dependence Modeling, 3, 126–140. The variety of proofs helps reveal the different structures behind the same inequality.

title: Chapter 4 — Insurance Pricing and Risk Measures
section: Why minimising ES is computationally convenient
text:
Why minimising ES is computationally convenient
The minimum representation is not only a proof device. Suppose a decision \(a\in\mathcal A\) determines a loss \(X_a\). The decision could represent portfolio holdings, reinsurance protection or exposure limits. We want to minimise \(\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X_a)\).
Formally, assuming the minima are attained,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{a\in\mathcal A}\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X_a)
&=\min_{a\in\mathcal A}\min_{t\in\mathbb R}
\left\{t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X_a-t)_+]\right\}\\
&=\min_{\substack{a\in\mathcal A\\t\in\mathbb R}}
\left\{t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X_a-t)_+]\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Without attainment, the same equality holds with infima. The central observation is simple: a minimum of minima is a joint minimum. We introduce the threshold as one additional decision variable and optimise it together with the portfolio. There is no need to recompute a quantile by a separate inner procedure for every trial portfolio.
For a finite collection of loss scenarios \(x_j(a)\) with probabilities \(p_j>0\), \(\sum_{j=1}^N p_j=1\), the objective becomes
\[
\min_{a,t}\left\{t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^N p_j(x_j(a)-t)_+\right\}.
\]
Introduce variables \(z_1,\ldots,z_N\) for the excess losses. The problem is equivalent to
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{minimise}\quad
&t+\frac1{1-\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^N p_jz_j\\
\text{over}\quad
&a\in\mathcal A,\quad t\in\mathbb R,\quad z_1,\ldots,z_N\in\mathbb R\\
\text{subject to}\quad
&z_j\geq x_j(a)-t\quad\text{and}\quad z_j\geq0,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,N.
\end{aligned}
\]
At an optimum, each \(z_j\) equals \((x_j(a)-t)_+\), because its coefficient in the objective is positive. If the scenario losses are affine in the decisions and the feasible set is described by linear constraints, this is a linear programme. If the losses are convex and the feasible set is convex, the joint problem remains convex. The treatment of atoms and fractional tail probabilities is automatic.
This is the practical force of the Rockafellar–Uryasev approach. The relevant references are Optimization of Conditional Value-at-Risk (2000) and Conditional Value-at-Risk for General Loss Distributions (2002).
The reformulation does not make every insurance decision easy: integer constraints, nonconvex contract structures or difficult loss models may remain. Nor does it remove the statistical difficulty of estimating rare losses. It does, however, give ES a particularly convenient optimisation structure once a tractable scenario model is available.
This is also why the distinction between VaR and ES matters beyond insurance. The Basel market-risk framework uses a 97.5% ES standard within its internal models approach, with further requirements on stress calibration and liquidity horizons. This differs from Solvency II’s one-year 99.5% VaR calibration: the measures, horizons and regulatory constructions should not be conflated.
